subject: Post-demo: Token flow trade-offs and key rotation plan for embed+tooling

Subject: Post-demo: Token flow trade-offs and key rotation plan for embed+tooling

Hi Alex — thanks again for the demo time this morning. Quick recap and concrete options for Elara's security/comms team to weigh in on.

Summary of ask from your side: secure production access for inference (embeddings + reranker + tool-calling) with minimal engineering lift, support for short-lived creds, and clear auditability. Below are three recommended flows with pros/cons and an initial rotation cadence: see attached elara_token_options.pdf for a one-page comparison.

1) Long-lived API keys (scoped per-environment)
   - Pros: simplest integration, immediate SDK compatibility, low latency.
   - Cons: higher blast radius if leaked; manual rotation unless backed by KMS; not ideal for external tool-calls that need per-request signing.

2) Service-account JWTs (short-lived signed tokens)
   - Pros: strong security model (short TTL), good for server-to-server flows, supports automated rotation via KMS/HSM and audit logs. SDKs can auto-refresh.
   - Cons: requires initial secret (signing key) management and a short-lived token exchange step. Slightly more integration effort.

3) OAuth 2.0 user/delegated flow (OIDC/JWT)
   - Pros: best for user-scoped actions and delegated tool-calls, integrates with IdP (Okta/GSuite).
   - Cons: more complex UX for non-interactive server processes; refresh tokens need careful handling.

Initial rotation recommendations (we can customize):
   - API keys: rotate every 30 days, with emergency revocation hooks.
   - Service-account signing keys: rotate key material every 90 days but issue tokens with 1 hour TTL; maintain a key epoch for backward verification.
   - OAuth: standard refresh token lifecycle per IdP, recommend 7-14 day refresh cadence for sensitive sessions.

Implications for the integration you saw:
   - Embeddings and reranker calls are high-volume; prefer short-lived tokens with automatic refresh to reduce leak surface.
   - Structured output/tool-calling: if Redwood or an external tool must act on behalf of Elara, we recommend signed JWTs to provide non-repudiation for tool actions.
   - Routing and per-route scoping: create route-level credentials or scopes so we can limit access to the reranker model vs. general generation endpoints.

Next steps (proposal):
   - Alex: confirm security team preference (1/2/3) and any mandated compliance reqs (HSM, SOC2 evidence).
   - Redwood: technical deep dive (60 mins) to scope SDK changes and rotation automation. Proposed slot: Thu 2028-09-21 10:00 PT.
   - Marissa: share sample rotation YAML and SDK implementation notes (attached).

Thanks — want to keep momentum. If helpful, Vanessa can scope Dedicated capacity/HSM procurement.

— Jonas
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Nice to meet you virtually, Alex — quick technical answers and a suggested implementation pattern. See rotation_sample.yaml attached for a concrete starter.

1) SDK token exchange/refresh model
   - Redwood SDK supports two common modes:
     a) Agent mode (recommended for server apps): you register a private signing key (HSM-backed recommended) with Redwood. The SDK exchanges the signing key for short-lived bearer tokens via a local refresher running in your infra (we supply the container). The refresh step is a lightweight token mint call and adds ~0.5–3ms to the first request when a new token is fetched; subsequent requests use cached tokens.
     b) Managed exchange (if you prefer Redwood-hosted token service): we can run the exchange in our Private deployment inside your VPC; requires additional onboarding but removes runbook burden.

2) Latency impact
   - For long-running flows (embeds/rerank): negligible after initial token fetch. Our benchmarks: steady-state per-token latency delta under 1% vs API keys when using in-process token caches. Batching reduces per-request crypto overhead.

3) Per-call signatures for tool-calling
   - Pattern: issue a short-lived JWT with claims that include request_id and call_scope; the receiving runtime verifies token signature against the signing key. This gives you non-repudiation and per-call auditability. Alternatively, for zero-trust we can integrate mTLS between Redwood and your tool endpoints.

Operational recommendations
   - TTL: 1-hour token TTL, rotate signing key material every 90 days. Keep at least one previous key for verification to avoid in-flight failures.
   - Scoping: create model-specific scopes (e.g., scope:models:rerank:prod) and enforce in Redwood routing policies.
   - Auditing: enable request-level audit logs and export to your SIEM (we support CloudWatch, Stackdriver, Splunk).

Attached: rotation_sample.yaml (example rotation policy and CI steps), and a short SDK snippet for automatic refresh. I can share a repo link in the deep dive.
